q: In the ionisation chamber of a mass spectrometer, atoms of the vaporised sample are usually turned into positive ions by:
o: Passing them through a strong magnetic field
Bombarding them with a beam of high-energy electrons
x: A beam of fast electrons knocks an electron out of each atom, giving positive ions. The electric plates only accelerate the ions and the magnetic field only separates them; mixing up these stages gives the tempting wrong answers.

q: A sample of neon gives peaks in its mass spectrum at m/e 20 and 22 only, with relative heights 9 : 1. The relative atomic mass of this neon is:
x: Weighted mean = (20 × 9 + 22 × 1)/10 = 202/10 = 20.2. Swapping the abundances gives 21.8, and taking a plain average of 20 and 22 gives 21.0.

q: Which pair of atoms contains the same number of neutrons?
x: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8. ¹²C/¹⁴N have 6 and 7, ⁴⁰Ar/⁴⁰Ca have 22 and 20, and ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl (isotopes) have 18 and 20; equal mass number or equal atomic number is the usual mix-up.

q: In a mass spectrometer, which ion has the same mass-to-charge ratio (m/e) as ¹⁶O⁺ and so follows the same path?
x: ¹⁶O⁺ has m/e = 16/1 = 16; ³²S²⁺ has 32/2 = 16. ³²S⁺ is 32, ¹⁶O²⁺ is 8 and ¹⁴N⁺ is 14. Looking only at the mass, or only at the element, gives the wrong choices.

q: Chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl by number of atoms. How many ³⁷Cl atoms are present in 0.1 mol of chlorine atoms? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
x: Total atoms = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²²; a quarter of them are ³⁷Cl: 6.02 × 10²² × 0.25 = 1.505 × 10²². Using 75% gives 4.515 × 10²² (the ³⁵Cl atoms), and forgetting the abundance gives 6.02 × 10²².

q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
x: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g. 100 g is the molar mass itself, and dividing instead of multiplying gives a far too small value.

q: How many electrons are present in 1.6 g of methane, CH₄? (H = 1, C = 12; Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
x: 1.6 g ÷ 16 g mol⁻¹ = 0.1 mol CH₄. Each molecule has 6 + 4 × 1 = 10 electrons, so 1 mol of electrons = 6.02 × 10²³. 6.02 × 10²² is the number of molecules (forgot the 10 electrons per molecule), and 3.01 × 10²³ is the number of atoms.

q: A gas has a density of 1.25 g dm⁻³ at STP. Which gas is it? (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: Molar mass = density × molar volume = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g mol⁻¹, which is N₂. O₂ (32 g mol⁻¹) would have a density of about 1.43 g dm⁻³; dividing 22.4 by 1.25 (about 18) points wrongly towards a light gas such as CH₄.

q: How many moles of ions in total are present in 11.1 g of calcium chloride, CaCl₂? (Ca = 40, Cl = 35.5)
x: Molar mass of CaCl₂ = 40 + 71 = 111 g mol⁻¹, so 11.1 g is 0.1 mol. Each formula unit gives one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻, i.e. 3 ions, so 0.3 mol of ions. 0.1 mol counts formula units only and 0.2 mol counts only the Cl⁻ ions.

q: What mass of sulphur dioxide, SO₂, contains the same number of oxygen atoms as 8.8 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16, S = 32)
x: 8.8 g CO₂ = 8.8/44 = 0.2 mol, holding 0.4 mol O atoms. SO₂ also has 2 O per molecule, so 0.2 mol SO₂ is needed = 0.2 × 64 = 12.8 g. Taking equal masses gives 8.8 g, and halving or doubling the mole ratio by mistake gives 6.4 g or 25.6 g.

q: In the combustion analysis of an organic compound that contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, the percentage of oxygen is usually found by:
o: Subtracting the percentages of carbon and hydrogen from 100
Weighing the oxygen absorbed by the magnesium perchlorate tube
Weighing the oxygen absorbed by the potash bulbs
Measuring the volume of oxygen gas given off
x: The absorbers only catch H₂O (magnesium perchlorate) and CO₂ (potash, KOH); oxygen is not measured directly, so %O = 100 − (%C + %H). Thinking that the absorbers trap oxygen is the usual slip.

q: A compound of nitrogen and oxygen contains 30.4% nitrogen by mass. Its empirical formula is: (N = 14, O = 16)
x: N : O = 30.4/14 : 69.6/16 = 2.17 : 4.35 = 1 : 2, so NO₂ (check: 14/46 = 30.4%). NO is 46.7% N and N₂O is 63.6% N; using mass ratios without dividing by atomic masses leads to the wrong formula.

q: Complete combustion of 1.5 g of an organic compound gives 2.2 g of CO₂. The percentage of carbon in the compound is: (C = 12, O = 16)
x: Mass of C = 2.2 × 12/44 = 0.6 g, so %C = 0.6/1.5 × 100 = 40%. 27.3% is just the carbon fraction of CO₂ (12/44), forgetting to relate it to the sample; 60% is the remaining percentage, not the carbon.

q: An oxide of iron contains 70% iron by mass. Its empirical formula is: (O = 16, Fe = 56)
x: Fe : O = 70/56 : 30/16 = 1.25 : 1.875 = 1 : 1.5 = 2 : 3, so Fe₂O₃ (check: 112/160 = 70%). FeO would be 77.8% Fe and Fe₃O₄ 72.4% Fe; stopping at the ratio 1 : 1.5 without making whole numbers is the common slip.

q: On strong heating, 24.6 g of hydrated magnesium sulphate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, leaves 12.0 g of anhydrous MgSO₄. The value of x is: (H = 1, O = 16, Mg = 24, S = 32)
x: MgSO₄ = 120 g mol⁻¹, so 12.0 g = 0.1 mol. Water lost = 24.6 − 12.0 = 12.6 g = 0.7 mol. x = 0.7/0.1 = 7. Dividing the mass of water by the mass of salt instead of using moles gives about 1, and assuming the familiar CuSO₄·5H₂O value gives 5.

q: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What mass of magnesium gives 0.1 mol of hydrogen gas? (Mg = 24)
x: Mg : H₂ = 1 : 1, so 0.1 mol Mg is needed = 0.1 × 24 = 2.4 g. Using the 2 in front of HCl doubles or halves the answer to 4.8 g or 1.2 g.

q: Aluminium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. What volume of hydrogen, measured at STP, is obtained from 5.4 g of aluminium? (Al = 27; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: 5.4/27 = 0.2 mol Al; Al : H₂ = 2 : 3, so 0.3 mol H₂ = 0.3 × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³. Taking Al : H₂ as 1 : 1 gives 4.48 dm³.

q: In a blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. What mass of iron is obtained from 16 g of Fe₂O₃? (O = 16, Fe = 56)
x: Fe₂O₃ = 160 g mol⁻¹, so 16 g = 0.1 mol, giving 0.2 mol Fe = 0.2 × 56 = 11.2 g. Forgetting the 2 Fe per Fe₂O₃ gives 5.6 g.

q: Ethane, C₂H₆, burns completely in oxygen to give CO₂ and H₂O. What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 10 dm³ of ethane, both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?
x: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. For gases at the same T and P, volume ratio = mole ratio, so O₂ = 10 × 7/2 = 35 dm³. Using 7 : 1 instead of 7 : 2 gives 70 dm³, and 20 dm³ is the volume of CO₂ formed.

q: A 8.4 g mixture of magnesium carbonate and sodium chloride is heated strongly until no more gas is given off: MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂ (NaCl does not change). 1.12 dm³ of CO₂, measured at STP, is collected. The percentage by mass of MgCO₃ in the mixture is: (C = 12, O = 16, Mg = 24; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: CO₂ = 1.12/22.4 = 0.05 mol, so MgCO₃ = 0.05 mol = 0.05 × 84 = 4.2 g. Percentage = 4.2/8.4 × 100 = 50%. Using the mass of CO₂ (2.2 g) in place of MgCO₃ gives about 26%, close to the 25% option.

q: 2.4 g of magnesium is added to a solution containing 0.15 mol of HCl: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What volume of hydrogen, measured at STP, is formed? (Mg = 24; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: Mg = 0.1 mol needs 0.2 mol HCl, but only 0.15 mol is present, so HCl is limiting. H₂ = 0.15/2 = 0.075 mol = 0.075 × 22.4 = 1.68 dm³. Working from Mg (the excess reactant) gives 2.24 dm³; ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio gives 3.36 dm³.

q: 4 g of methane is burned in a closed vessel with 32 g of oxygen: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Which reactant is in excess, and what mass of it is left over? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
x: CH₄ = 4/16 = 0.25 mol needs 0.5 mol O₂ (16 g). O₂ present = 32/32 = 1 mol, so 0.5 mol (16 g) of O₂ is left. Taking O₂ : CH₄ as 1 : 1 leaves 24 g; thinking CH₄ is in excess is the mass-not-moles slip.

q: 11.2 g of iron is heated with 8.0 g of sulphur, Fe + S → FeS, and 13.2 g of FeS is obtained. The percentage yield is: (S = 32, Fe = 56)
x: Fe = 0.2 mol and S = 0.25 mol; they react 1 : 1, so Fe is limiting. Theoretical FeS = 0.2 × 88 = 17.6 g; yield = 13.2/17.6 × 100 = 75%. Using sulphur as limiting gives 22 g and 60%; comparing with the total mass of reactants (19.2 g) gives about 69%.

q: The actual yield of a product is usually less than its theoretical yield mainly because:
o: The excess reactant is left unreacted at the end
Mass is destroyed during the chemical reaction
Some product is lost during separation and purification, or side reactions occur
The theoretical yield is always calculated from the excess reactant
x: Losses while filtering, transferring and purifying, and side reactions giving other products, reduce the amount actually collected. A leftover excess reactant is normal and does not lower the yield; mass is conserved; and the theoretical yield is worked out from the limiting reactant.
